entry.title: A tour of the example content
entry.content:
This post is a longer, flowing piece of prose. It exists because most of the other posts in the example content are short demonstrations that jump straight from one construct to the next, while real writing is mostly paragraphs.

Why longer text matters

A real post is not a list of features. It is a sequence of paragraphs, each building on the last, with the occasional heading to give the reader a place to rest and a way to find their place again. Short posts do not exercise the styles that make longer text comfortable to read: the space between paragraphs, the measure of a line, and the way a heading clears the text around it.

So this post stretches those styles. It also, as a matter of course, mixes in several of the constructs the example content demonstrates elsewhere, so they can be seen working together rather than in isolation.

The example content at a glance

The example content is organized into a handful of groups, each focused on one area of the generator’s input:

Group Focus
prose Core Markdown text, lists, and footnotes
tables The four Pandoc table syntaxes
code Syntax highlighting and math
languages Language front matter, CJK, and ruby
elements Raw HTML, forms, and controls

A note on footnotes

Footnotes keep an aside out of the flow of a sentence.1 They are useful in longer writing, where a sentence needs a caveat that would otherwise interrupt the argument.

Code in prose

Longer writing also leaves room for a short code block without it feeling forced:

main :: IO ()
main = putStrLn "An example"

And a quote, for good measure:

A paragraph is not a luxury; it is the basic unit of argument.

Where to go next

From here, the other groups show the remaining features in detail: the languages posts for ruby and CJK, the tables posts for table syntax, and the elements posts for raw HTML and controls.

  1. Like this one, which is an inline footnote. It stays near its marker, and a back-link returns the reader to where they left off.↩︎

entry.title: Smart typography
entry.content:
Pandoc rewrites punctuation as it parses.

What gets rewritten

“Double quotes” and ‘single quotes’ become curly, two hyphens – become an en dash, three — become an em dash, and trailing dots… become an ellipsis.

Escaping

A backslash keeps characters literal: -- stays two hyphens, ... stays three dots. Code spans are never rewritten: --flag.

Subscript and superscript

Water is H2O and a square is x2. This is separate from math, which uses $...$.

entry.title: Lists
entry.content:
Lists come in several flavours.

Bulleted and ordered

  • one item
  • another item
    • a nested item
    • another nested item
  • back to the top level
  1. first
  2. second
  3. third

Ordered lists with a start value

Any number starts the list at that value:

  1. Starts at three.
  2. Then four.

Task lists

Example lists

Mark a list with (@) for an “example” list:

  1. First example.
  2. Second example.

Fancy lists

A letter or roman numeral controls the numbering:

  1. Lowercase letters.
  2. Keep going.
  1. Roman numerals.
  2. Continue.

Line blocks

A line block preserves line breaks:

A line block
keeps each line
   and leading spaces
   on its own line.

Definition lists

A definition rendered as a <dl>.

entry.title: Formatting
entry.content:
This post demonstrates the core prose constructs: headings, emphasis, links, quotes, code, and footnotes.

Headings

Headings start at level two here, because the page template already renders the title as the single level-one heading. A section can nest further.

A subsection

Subsections descend one level at a time.

A sub-subsection

And keep descending, with no skipped levels.

A fifth-level heading

Still descending.

A sixth-level heading

The deepest level.

Paragraphs and line breaks

A paragraph is a run of text. A line break is forced with two trailing spaces.
Like this one.

Emphasis

Text can be emphasized, strong, deleted, or shown as inline code.

Links

Links can point to a page, to a section, to an external site, or to an email.

Blockquotes

A blockquote contains quoted text.

It can nest another level.

And return to the first level.

Code

An indented code block:

def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name

A fenced block with a language:

def greet(name):
    return "Hello, " + name

A horizontal rule

A rule separates sections.

Notes

A sentence with an inline footnote.1 And one with a reference footnote.2

  1. An inline footnote stays near its marker.↩︎

  2. A reference footnote defined at the end of the document.↩︎
